paras: The lynching of Garfield McCoy, Wiley Anette and George McKinney took place early on June 26, 1903, when a mob took the three Black men from the jail at Newton, Baker County, Georgia, hanged them from one tree a mile west of town and fired hundreds of shots into their bodies. They were awaiting trial for the murder of F. S. Bullard, a white farmer shot at a dance on his farm the previous Saturday. Editors in and outside Georgia noted that the men had not been lynched for the "usual crime" and that their trial had never been in doubt.

On Saturday night, June 20, Black people from several counties gathered for a "frolic" at the house of one of Bullard's tenants near Peace. Accounts differ: the Savannah Morning News said Bullard went to stop a "free-for-all fight," the New York Sun that he asked a drunken crowd for quiet, and the Macon Telegraph that the three put out the lights. All said McCoy, Anette and McKinney, described as Miller County men, fired on Bullard with revolvers, and that he died on Tuesday.
Arrested on Monday, the three were held at Newton for superior court after a commitment hearing at which, the Telegraph reported, testimony showed McKinney fired the fatal shot.

About midnight Bailiff R. C. Tucker woke Jailer William Screws, saying he had a prisoner to lock up. When Screws unlocked the jail, armed men thrust a pistol in his face and made him open the cell; in the confusion Tucker's prisoner escaped, while another inmate, James Story, was left alone. According to the Telegraph, the men's "appeals for mercy" were ignored and the mob beat and slapped them with knives as they left the jail.

With their hands tied, the three were hanged together from one limb a mile west of town. The mob fired several hundred shots into the bodies and quietly dispersed. The Telegraph counted fifty men in the mob; the Savannah account described "a dozen men" springing on the jailer.

Screws, also the coroner, empaneled an inquest jury that morning but, the Sun reported, recognized no one in the mob. Georgia reports called the lynching unexpected and "generally deplored," blaming the plight of Bullard's invalid wife and small children for inflaming feeling. Ten days later the Birmingham Age-Herald was still urging that the Newton "ringleaders" be arrested and indicted; no report of an inquest verdict or arrest appears in the coverage.

The first notice, an Atlanta dispatch in the New York Evening World on June 26, said only that three Black men had been lynched at Newton for an unknown crime. Fuller Albany dispatches ran on June 27 in the New-York Tribune ("MOB LYNCHES THREE"), the Sun and the Savannah Morning News, and South Carolina weeklies reprinted them.

Georgia papers treated guilt as settled: the Savannah Morning News headlined "GUILTY NEGROES PAID WITH THEIR LIVES," and the Dawson News wrote of "Murderers of White Farmer" who "Made Exit by Rope Route." The Savannah paper nonetheless argued editorially that "the law ought to have been permitted to take its course," while the Pelham Journal, which it quoted, concluded that "The remedy lies with the culprit."

Outside Georgia, a Chicago Tribune editorial reprinted in the Washington Evening Star as "The Lynching Madness" saw "no question of the failure of justice," and the Birmingham Age-Herald accused Governor Terrell of "winking one eye at the lynchers."

The Black papers in the coverage ran wire copy without comment. The Baltimore Afro-American printed the Telegraph dispatch under "MURDER WAS SPEEDILY AVENGED," and the Savannah Tribune ran the same text, calling the men "negroes who murdered F. S. Bullard," that the white Bamberg Herald had printed two days earlier. The Professional World carried the short Atlanta notice, and the Indianapolis Freeman listed "Three Negroes, Newton, Ga." among June's lynchings.

Anette's name also appears as "Annette" and "Arnette." The Savannah dispatch reported "some talk of a lynching" beforehand; the Telegraph said there was "absolutely no talk of lynching." The Pelham Journal's claim that the three also killed "five negroes" appears in no news report; the Savannah dispatch mentioned six Black people wounded at the dance but no other deaths.

bases: A mob took three Black prisoners charged with murder from the Newton jail, hanged them and shot their bodies (A5, A6, A8).

Three men were hanged and shot by a mob of fifty (A5, A14) or at least a dozen (A8) that seized them from the jailer at pistol point, acting without authority to punish them for the alleged murder of F. S. Bullard (A6, A8).
Separate Albany dispatches in the Sun (A6), the Savannah Morning News (A8) and the Macon Telegraph (A5, A14), plus an Atlanta dispatch (A7), agree on the seizure, the hanging and the shooting.

accounts.label: Macon Telegraph's Albany dispatch
accounts.gist: Mob of fifty took the men about 2 a.m. after a bailiff's ruse, beat them with knives, hanged them a mile west of town amid shouts and fired several hundred shots; carried by white papers and by the Baltimore Afro-American.

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News's Albany dispatch
accounts.gist: A dozen men sprang on the jailer at midnight; the men were hanged with hemp rope from one limb; the mob had planned quietly and the lynching was deplored locally; the men's guilt treated as established.

accounts.label: The Sun's Albany dispatch
accounts.gist: Lynching 'last night'; the mob was thought to come from Bullard's section; Screws as coroner empaneled an inquest but recognized no one.

accounts.label: Atlanta brief
accounts.gist: Early report on 'meager' information that three Black men had been lynched at Newton.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headlined 'GUILTY NEGROES PAID WITH THEIR LIVES' and called the killing of Bullard 'cowardly', then editorially deplored the lynching and said the law should have taken its course.
The Pelham Journal, quoted in Savannah, deplored lynch law but said 'The remedy lies with the culprit'.
The Chicago Tribune (via the Evening Star) and Birmingham Age-Herald used the case against lynching, the latter blaming Governor Terrell.
Northern dailies ran wire dispatches under headlines such as 'MOB LYNCHES THREE' and 'THREE HANGED ON ONE TREE'.
The Professional World, Baltimore Afro-American ('MURDER WAS SPEEDILY AVENGED') and Savannah Tribune ran white wire copy, including 'negroes who murdered F. S. Bullard', without comment.
The Indianapolis Freeman listed the case in its roll of June lynchings.
